Chapter 03

The map: every feature, and where it earns its place

A list of everything in Svelte 5 and SvelteKit 3 that Abacus uses — runes, snippets, attachments, remote functions, live queries, hooks, the environment layer, the September and October 2026 additions — and the chapter where each one is for something.

By the end of this chapter

Have a map of the framework as this project uses it, so you can read the course in any order and know what you are looking at.

This is the chapter to come back to. Each row is a feature, what it is for in Abacus, and where it lives. Nothing here is a demo; if you cannot find the row that names a feature, the project does not use it, and that is deliberate too.

Svelte 5

  • $state — the sheet’s selection, title, version and editing state (ch. 15); toasts; every page’s local state. $state.raw — a value that is replaced and never changed inside: the live connection’s status, a small tagged union (ch. 28). $state.eager — once, in the header: with async Svelte a navigation’s updates wait for the new page’s awaits, and the current-link highlight reads the incoming pathname eagerly so the link somebody just clicked lights up at once (ch. 30).
  • $derived and $derived.by — the grid’s geometry from scroll position and sizes (ch. 19); the formula bar’s coloured segments, the syntax error, the completion list (ch. 21); and, as fields of a class, the nine cells of the reactivity lesson and whether each one is on a cycle (ch. 17). A $derived that a handler assigns to — the completion highlight, the find index — as a reset without an effect.
  • $effect — exactly where a side effect is the point: scrolling the active cell into view, clearing flash highlights after a timer, following the live query for as long as its stream lasts, and tearing the live connection down (ch. 19, 33).
  • $props — every component. $props.id() — the ids the formula bar’s combobox points at, unique per instance and the same on the server and in the browser (ch. 21). bind:this on a component to call its exported insertAtCaret (ch. 21). $bindable is not used: no component here offers two-way binding as its API.
  • Snippets with parameters — the grid renders one cell snippet in four layers: the body, frozen rows, frozen columns, the frozen corner (ch. 19). {@render extra?.()} lets a page put its own buttons in the toolbar.
  • Attachments — {@attach cinematic()} on the landing page (ch. 31); focusing an input on mount in the cell editor and find bar (ch. 21, 22).
  • Function bindings — bind:textContent={get, set} on the editable title (ch. 32).
  • bind:files with a DataTransfer to clear a file input so the same file can be chosen twice (ch. 22).
  • <svelte:boundary> around every await in markup, with pending for the first load and failed wherever a failure should stay where it happened: the workspace list and the passkey list say what went wrong and offer Try again, the header falls back to a Sign in chip, the profile offers Try again, the local sheet keeps its sign-in link, and the template page’s save button simply does not appear (ch. 30, 31, 32, 34). failed is handed the App.Error that handleError made rather than whatever was thrown, and failureOf reads it (ch. 29). The stored sheet’s own await getSheet(…) has no boundary on purpose: without the record there is no page, and +error.svelte is the right answer (ch. 33). And one place there is deliberately none: a reactive cell in the lesson, because an exception inside a $derived goes to the boundary of the effect that created it (ch. 17).
  • Declaration tags — a plain {const spec = FUNCTIONS.get(name)} where the value is fixed for as long as its block lives: the lesson’s cell names, a .for(id) form per card, a function’s description per suggestion, the cell editor’s session. {const x = $derived(…)} where it must follow state: the grid’s cells, and every await in markup — the workspace list, the settings profile, “who am I” in the header (ch. 19, 30, 34).
  • SvelteMap/SvelteSet — column widths, row heights and flash highlights, where fine-grained reactivity is wanted; a plain Map in the engine, where it is not (ch. 15).
  • untrack — reading the initial data once so a later change cannot throw away edits (ch. 33); starting the live loop without making its effect depend on every message (ch. 28); the scroll position the active-cell effect is about to change (ch. 19).
  • hydratable — the landing page’s random dots, computed once on the server and reused by the client so hydration does not repaint them (ch. 31).
  • createSubscriber is not used; the live connection is a query.live, which does that job.

SvelteKit 3

  • The environment layer — defineEnvVars in src/env.ts, with valibot schemas, a public flag you have to type, and a static variable that is inlined at build time; a declared variable is imported from $app/env/private or $app/env/public (this chapter, below).
  • #lib — every import of the project’s own code: Node’s subpath imports, declared in package.json, with the file’s real extension (this chapter, below).
  • Remote functions — query for reads, form for anything a page without JavaScript must still be able to do, command for everything else, and query.live for the collaboration stream, iterated with for await (ch. 26–28). requested(q, n).refreshAll(), withOverride, .for(id), .preflight(), .enhance(), invalid(issue.field(…)), and redirect from inside a form handler all appear where they are needed (ch. 27, 34).
  • Hooks from @sveltejs/kit/hooks — sequence, a preload filter that names font files by source filename, a per-route Content Security Policy swap, handleFetch, handleError told apart by kind on the server and in the browser, init, transport (ch. 29).
  • Two shapes of client error — a remote call awaited in a handler rejects with an HttpError whose sentence is body.message, and messageOf reads it for every toast; a boundary is handed an App.Error, read as error.message (ch. 29, 34).
  • Universal load that calls remote queries — the sheet page (ch. 33); csr = false pages that ship no JavaScript (ch. 35); prerender with entries() for the templates (ch. 31).
  • A layout reset — +page@.svelte for the embed, which must not inherit the app shell (ch. 35).
  • +server.ts handlers — a streamed CSV response, a QUERY handler, a health check (ch. 35).
  • $app/state — page, navigating, updated; the version poll that offers a reload after a deploy (ch. 30).
  • adapter-node 6 — paths.origin baked in, SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT, BODY_SIZE_LIMIT, a Dockerfile that runs as node and migrates before it listens (ch. 38).

What the September 2026 releases added, and where

  • router.resolution: 'server' — the config (ch. 02), and the navigation test that proves it (ch. 37).
  • Fonts in the preload filter with their source filename — hooks.server.ts names the two files the first paint needs (ch. 29).
  • handleError with kind and issues — a validation failure logs the field path and answers with a plain message; only an unknown error gets a correlation id (ch. 29).
  • Hook types from @sveltejs/kit/hooks — every hook file imports them from there, and the comment in hooks.server.ts says what the old import from @sveltejs/kit does now: a type error for every name (ch. 29).
  • query.live with .current, .connected, .reconnect() and for await — the whole of chapter 28, and the reconnect button on the sheet page (ch. 33).
  • requested(q, n).refreshAll() in a form handler — deleting a sheet from the workspace (ch. 27).

What the October 2026 release — SvelteKit 3.0 — changed, and where

  • #lib instead of $lib — the alias for src/lib is now Node’s own subpath imports, declared in package.json and resolved natively by Vite and TypeScript, with the file’s real extension (this chapter, below).
  • $app/env/private and $app/env/public — every environment variable is declared once in src/env.ts and imported from one of these, in place of the four deprecated $env/… modules (this chapter, below).
  • resolve() on every link, with a route id — /(app)/sheets, layout group included; a renamed folder is a type error in every link to it, and no-navigation-without-resolve keeps it that way (ch. 30). Pathnames lost their leading slash, which is why the project uses route ids only.
  • match() before goto() — SvelteKit 3’s goto rejects a URL that is not a route, so the sign-in page asks the router about ?next= first and falls back to the workspace (ch. 34).
  • Response.json(…) — the platform’s own, in place of the deprecated json() helper; the API and the health check (ch. 35).
  • Vitest 5 — an inline project inherits the config that declares it, so the two projects lost their extends lines (ch. 02, 36).
  • adapter-node 6.0 — static assets are served from a list recorded at build time, with content-hash ETags and no Last-Modified, and only to GET and HEAD; a file dropped into build/client after the build is not served, which is the right answer for an image that is built once (ch. 38).
  • pnpm 12 — a release-age delay before a freshly published version is installed; pnpm-workspace.yaml records the ones taken early, and says why (ch. 38).

The environment layer, since every chapter reads it

A variable not declared here cannot be imported — a type error at build time rather than an undefined in production three weeks later. public: true is something you have to type, so a secret cannot reach the browser by accident. PUBLIC_ORIGIN is static, and the comment gives the two reasons: the CSRF check and the passkey relying-party id both need build and run to agree.

Environment variables are always strings, and the place to turn one into a number is here — once — rather than in every file that reads it with a Number() and a hopeful default. The bounds are opinions with reasons attached, which is what a bound should be.

This is what using one looks like: the top of the module that stores sheets. CELL_LIMIT arrives from $app/env/private already a number, already checked. private is the half the browser can never import — a client file that tries is a build error — and $app/env/public is the other half, for variables declared with public: true. The same block shows the other convention you will meet in every file: the project’s own modules are imported as #lib/sheet/apply.ts, with the real extension.

Why the environment is imported from $app/env and not $env

SvelteKit 2 had four magic modules — $env/static/private, $env/static/public, $env/dynamic/private, $env/dynamic/public — and you chose one by asking two questions at every import: is it secret, and is it known at build time? The answers were scattered across the codebase, and a variable nobody declared was simply undefined until it mattered. SvelteKit 3 asks both questions once, in src/env.ts: public: true answers the first, static: true the second, and the schema says what a valid value is. The import is then only $app/env/private or $app/env/public, and an undeclared name is a type error. The $env/… modules still exist, deprecated; this project does not use them.

The toolchain

Every #lib/… import in the project resolves through these two lines. A specifier starting with # is a subpath import: Node’s own way for a package to give its internal folders a name, declared in its package.json and private to it. #lib/sheet/apply.ts means ./src/lib/sheet/apply.ts, and Vite, TypeScript and Node all read the declaration themselves — no plugin, no paths in tsconfig.json. The bare #lib line points at an index.js this project does not have, because nothing imports the folder itself; it is the line SvelteKit’s migration guide gives, and it costs nothing until somebody does.

Why #lib, and why the imports name .ts files

Until SvelteKit 3 the alias was $lib, and SvelteKit configured it behind your back — which meant every tool that was not SvelteKit, from a test runner to a script run with plain node, needed telling about it separately. #lib is a Node feature, so every tool that understands Node packages understands it already: from the project folder, plain node with no flags and no configuration runs import('#lib/sheet/templates.ts') and gets the same module the app does. The extension is written out because that is what the file is called. Node runs TypeScript directly now and resolves paths exactly; a guess from apply to apply.ts or apply/index.ts is a bundler’s habit, and code that relies on it only runs inside the bundler.

check type-checks the app and the worker — the CSV importer runs where window does not exist, so it has its own tsconfig.worker.json with the WebWorker library instead of the DOM one. verify is the gate: type-check, lint, unit and browser tests, build, and the end-to-end suite on a desktop and a phone profile. Everything in this course passed it.

extends names $app/tsconfig, the base config SvelteKit regenerates on every svelte-kit sync — module resolution, the DOM libraries, the route types — so this file says only what is specific to the project. noUncheckedIndexedAccess is the flag this project would choose if it could choose one. A spreadsheet is a grid of maybes — a row that may not exist, a token after the last token — and every one of those is a crash at runtime or a red squiggle now.

Checkpoint

  • You can name, from memory, three Svelte 5 features and the chapter where each is used for something.
  • You can say why PUBLIC_ORIGIN is static: true and SESSION_SECRET is not public.
  • You know which file type-checks the worker and why it needs a different library.
